extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, inventors, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to draft and how courts evaluate patent specifications: what must be described, what may be referred to as old, enablement, best mode, claim scope, and how ambiguities are treated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings and words must be read together
rubrics_metrics.description: The drawings are to be taken in connection with the words, and if by a comparison of the words and the drawings, the one would explain the other sufficiently to enable a skilful mechanic to perform the work, the specification is sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings may supply details omitted from text so long as, when read together, they enable a skilled mechanic to practice the invention. The specification can be sufficient by combination of text and figures even if either alone would be inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description — distinguish old from new
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute requires the patentee to give 'a written description of his invention or discovery.' This involves the necessity ... of distinguishing between what is old and what is new. He is required to point out in what his invention or discovery consists; and if he includes in his description what has been invented before, without showing that he does not claim to have invented that, his patent will be broader than his invention, and therefore void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must identify the novel subject-matter and, where prior art is used, clearly indicate that such portions are not claimed. Failure to distinguish may render the patent broader than the inventor's actual invention and invalidate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims are indivisible — if any claimed subject is old, patent may be void
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever appears to be covered by the claim of the patentee, as his own invention, must be taken as part of the claim, for courts of law are not at liberty to reject any part of the claim; and therefore if it turns out that anything claimed is not new, the patent is void, however small or unimportant such asserted invention may be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafters must avoid claiming things that include prior art. Courts will not excise invalid portions of a claim — the presence of any non-novel claimed element can void the whole claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction to be co-extensive with actual discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification should be so construed, as, consistently with the fair import of language, will make the claim co-extensive with the actual discovery. So that, a patentee, unless his language necessarily imports a claim of things in use, will be presumed not to intend to claim things which he must know to be in use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation should, if possible, align claim scope with what the inventor actually discovered; ambiguous language will be construed against a claim that would appropriate known, in-use items.

rubrics_metrics.name: State distinctly what is claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of the distinction between what is new and what is old is to show distinctly what the patentee claims as his invention ... The patentee is not confined to any precise form of words. The more usual form is to state affirmatively what the patentee claims as new, and if he makes use of anything old, to state negatively that he does not claim that thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification should clearly and unambiguously set out the subject-matter claimed. Affirmative statements of new features plus explicit disclaimers of known elements are common and effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not appropriate prior art; identify old/immaterial parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee must not only claim neither more nor less than his own invention, but he must not appear even unintentionally to appropriate to himself any part which is old, or has been used in other manufactures. Those parts that are old and immaterial, or are not of the essence of the invention, should either not be mentioned, or should be named only to be designated as old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When including known elements in the specification, either omit unnecessary prior-art details or expressly label them as old to avoid implying novelty in those parts. Describing irrelevant known parts as essential risks a construction against the patentee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known things may be referred to generally if not ambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: In describing what is old, it is not always necessary to enter into detail. Things generally known, or in common use, may be referred to in general terms, provided they create no ambiguity or uncertainty, and provided such reference is accompanied by an intelligible description of what is new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It's permissible to reference common, well-known components broadly, but only when that general reference will not create uncertainty about what the actual invention is and is paired with clear disclosure of the new aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: When improving a machine, set out prior art and then disclaim it
rubrics_metrics.description: In describing an improvement of a machine ... the former machine ... should be set forth in the patent sufficiently to make known ... what it is that the patentee engrafts his improvement upon; he should then disclaim the invention of the thing thus referred to or described, and state distinctly his improvement as the thing which he claims to have invented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For improvements, explain the existing machine enough to show the context, but explicitly disclaim prior parts and then clearly describe the particular improvement being claimed to avoid overclaiming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vagueness in the manner of description
rubrics_metrics.description: A common defect consists in that sort of vagueness and ambiguity in the manner of describing the invention, which makes it difficult or impossible to determine what the invention is. This is an objection distinct from an ambiguity in the terms made use of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafters should avoid procedural or structural vagueness (unclear steps, indeterminate instructions) even if individual terms are precise; vagueness that prevents identification of the invention can be fatal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic claims must be enabled across the claimed class
rubrics_metrics.description: If it be stated that a whole class of substances may be used to produce a given effect, when, in fact, only one is capable of being so used, an ambiguity is at once produced, and the public are misled; but, if the patentee states the substances which he makes use of himself, and there are still other substances which will produce the effect, and he claims them by a generic description ... his claim will not be void for ambiguity, or too broad ... provided the combination is new in respect to all the substances thus referred to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad/generic claims to a class are permissible only if the specification either (a) actually enables the class, or (b) the inventor discloses the exemplars he uses and the claim is honestly supported by novelty across the class. Otherwise claiming an inoperative class element is ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claiming substitutes and multiple modes — allowed if disclosed and new
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent act ... does not limit the inventor to one single mode, or one single set of ingredients, to carry into effect his invention. He may claim as many modes, as he pleases, provided always, that the claim is limited to such, as he has invented, and as are substantially new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may claim alternative structures, substitutes, or multiple modes of performing the invention, but only to the extent those alternatives are actually within what you have invented and are novel. The patentee should describe the modes he contemplates as best, although he need not enumerate every conceivable formal variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory duty to explain principle and several modes
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of a machine, that the inventor shall fully explain the principle, and the several modes, in which he has contemplated the application of that principle, by which it may be distinguished from other inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must disclose the underlying principle of the invention and the principal modes of applying it — this is a statutory/essential disclosure requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction is for the court; enablement is for the fact-finder
rubrics_metrics.description: The question whether the specification discloses what the invention is, is a question for the court on construction of the patent; while the question whether it sufficiently describes the mode of carrying the invention into practice, is a question for the jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal interpretation of claims is judicial; factual questions about whether a skilled person can practice the invention from the disclosure are matters of fact (historically jury). Drafting should thus both aim for clear claim language and factual sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement — must give clear and specific directions to a skilled mechanic
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the most common defects in a specification consists in want of clear or specific directions, which will enable a mechanic to make the thing described. A specification may be perfectly sufficient, as to the point of stating what the invention is, and yet the directions for making the thing may be so vague and indefinite, as not to enable a skilful mechanic to accomplish the object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide practical, concrete instructions and proportions/modes where necessary. Lack of such enabling detail may defeat both validity and the ability to prove infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to disclose best mode and advantageous circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee is bound to disclose the most advantageous mode known to him; and any circumstance conducive to the advantageous operation of his invention; and it is a correlative of this rule, that if things wholly useless and unnecessary are introduced into the specification, as if they were essential ... the patent may be declared void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose the best way you know to practice the invention and material details that make it work well. Introducing irrelevant or useless material presented as essential creates a presumption of bad faith and risks invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden to show later improvements were post-issue
rubrics_metrics.description: There is one case where it seems to have been held that an improved mode of working his machine by the patentee, different from the specification of his patent, casts upon him the burthen of showing that he made the improvement subsequently to the issuing of his patent, otherwise it will be presumed that he did not disclose in his specification the best method known to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If asserting best-mode compliance where patentee later used a better method, be prepared to prove the later improvement post-dated the patent; otherwise the omission may be treated as failure to disclose the best mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must enable determination of infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: An infringement will not have taken place, unless the invention can be practised completely by following the specification; if the patent does not fully describe everything essential to the making or doing of the thing patented, there will be no infringement by the fresh maker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To sustain infringement, the patented invention must be sufficiently disclosed so that a later practitioner could practice it from the specification; an incomplete spec may preclude an infringement finding even if the accused device performs the same general principle.
